messages.author: 9cd7abbc55138f90
messages.subject: Overhead of pbdR
parts:
Hello,
       Since pbdSLAP calls ScaLAPACK routines in R, there must be some overhead in it. How about the overhead introduced by pbdR? It is very significant? I find few performance benchmarks online about the pbdSLAP compared to a native Fortran/C program who calls ScaLAPACK directly. Can anyone provide some information on that? Thank you again.

Best wishes,
                                    Dale Wang

messages.author: 04ee6652802764c3
messages.subject: Re: Overhead of pbdR
parts:
Hi Dale,

Not sure which benchmarks you're referring to.  There is of course some overhead in calling things from R; the size of this overhead largely depends on the operation.  For very shallow wrappers, like matrix-matrix multiply `%*%` and singular value decomposition La.svd(), the overhead is pretty small, and doesn't really scale with the problem size.  For other operations, (covariance, subsetting, linear regression, ...), these include a lot of additional work (most of which is written in Fortran, by the way), and aren't immediately comparable to a simple benchmark of native routines. 

I've profiled svd extensively, and have never seen more than a fraction of a second in overhead compared to calling the function natively.  This discounts the startup time for R itself, which can be significant, but is also fixed.  Long story short, if your problem is "small", I don't think pbdDMAT is a very good fit.  You're almost certainly going to be better off using R linked with multi-threaded BLAS (MKL, OpenBLAS, ACML, ...).  For much larger problems, and especially when the problem requires more memory than is available on one node, pbdDMAT begins to win (you can of course combine the two approaches as well).

-Drew

messages.subject: Re: Overhead of pbdR
parts: "Overhead of pbdR" is a misleading subject for this content. pbdSLAP is a part of pbdR. Define your problem first, then "overhead" and "significant" followed in terms of pbdSLAP rather than pbdR.
